title: Poker Simulation
text:
As an avid golfer, I have bore witness to 4 holes-in-one and have been gifted with 3 of my own. As an inexperienced poker player, however, I have yet to receive witness anyone receiving a four-of-a-kind. Given its seemingly elusive nature, I was interested in finding out the probability of being dealt a four-of-a-kind, and if/how the probability changes based on the number of players playing.
To calculate the probability, I created a simulation of Texas hold ’em, the most popular variety of poker with the following rules:
“Two cards, known as hole cards, are dealt face down to each player, and then five community cards are dealt face up in three stages. The stages consist of a series of three cards (‘the flop’), later an additional single card (‘the turn’ or ‘fourth street’), and a final card (‘the river’ or ‘fifth street’).”
“In all casinos, the dealer will burn a card before the flop, turn, and river.”
- Texas hold ’em - Wikipedia
I began by creating a function to simulate the movement of cards in a game of Texas hold ’em with n players (dealing to players, burning, dealing community cards).


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tictoc)
poker_game <- function(n = 4){
  
  deck <- 1:52
  players <- n
  #dealing to each player one card at a time
  #deal one card to myself first
  hand1 <- sample(deck, 1, replace = FALSE)
  #remove dealt card from the deck
  deck <- setdiff(deck, hand1)
  
  #deal one card to the rest of the players, remove from deck
  deck <- setdiff(deck, sample(deck, players-1, replace = FALSE))
  
  #deal second card to myself
  hand1 <- append(hand1, sample(deck, 1, replace = FALSE))
  deck <- setdiff(deck, hand1)
  
  #deal second card to the rest of the players
  deck <- setdiff(deck, sample(deck, players-1, replace = FALSE))
  
  #burn one card before the flop
  deck <- setdiff(deck, sample(deck, 1, replace = FALSE))
  
  #deal the flop
  flop <- sample(deck, 3, replace = FALSE)
  deck <- setdiff(deck, flop)
  
  #burn one card before the turn
  deck <- setdiff(deck, sample(deck, 1, replace = FALSE))
  
  #deal the turn
  turn <- sample(deck, 1, replace = FALSE)
  deck <- setdiff(deck, turn)
  
  #burn one card before the river
  deck <- setdiff(deck, sample(deck, 1, replace = FALSE))
  
  #deal the river
  river <- sample(deck, 1, replace = FALSE)
#  deck <- setdiff(deck, river)
  
  #returns my hand plus the community cards
  return(append(hand1, append(flop, append(turn, river))))
}

#simulates my hand in a game of poker with four players
poker_game(4)


[1] 49 12 46 19 45 26  9


The output above represents the hand dealt to the player. The deck is generated as a vector of integers from 1 to 52, and each “card’s” face value is determined by its number modulus 13. If we get four cards for which their representative number mod 13 are equal, then we have gotten four-of-a-kind.
Next, I created a function to check if a hand has four-of-a-kind.


Code
four_of_a_kind <- function(nada, hand = poker_game(4)){
  card_values <- hand %% 13
  any(table(card_values) == 4)
}
four_of_a_kind(hand = poker_game(4)) |> print()


[1] FALSE


The output above indicates whether the hand inputted into the function contains a four-of-a-kind.
The next step is to simulate many poker games to get an approximate probability of being dealt a four-of-a-kind.


Code
set.seed(47)
n <- 100000

tic()
odds_map <- map_lgl(c(1:n), ~ four_of_a_kind(nada = .x))
toc()


31.12 sec elapsed


Code
mean(odds_map)


[1] 0.00161


The above output is the estimated probability of being dealt a four-of-a-kind in a poker game with four players.
After simulating 100,000 poker games, I found that, in a game with four players, the odds of being dealt a four-of-a-kind are about 0.168%, or about 1 in 600. Given I have played approximately ~60 hands of poker, it makes sense that I have yet to receive a four-of-a-kind.
Given the above findings, I wanted to know if I would be less likely to receive a four-of-a-kind in a game with more players, given that cards I need for a four-of-a-kind could be dealt to other players.
To find out if this is the case, I ran the simulation over poker games with 2 through 8 players and plotted the findings below:


Code
set.seed(47)
n <- 100000
tic()
results <- map_dfr(2:8, function(x) {
  prob <- mean(map_lgl(1:n, ~ four_of_a_kind(nada = .x)))  # Probability estimation
  tibble(players = x, probability = prob)
})
toc()


218.11 sec elapsed


Code
print(results)


# A tibble: 7 × 2
  players probability
    <int>       <dbl>
1       2     0.00161
2       3     0.0018 
3       4     0.0017 
4       5     0.00156
5       6     0.00144
6       7     0.00176
7       8     0.0017 


The above table shows the probabilities of being dealt a four-of-a-kind in poker games with 2-8 players. There is no clear trend in the probabilities across multiple runs of the simulation. I would run a higher number of iterations (i.e. n = 1,000,000) to get more precise probabilities but the n = 100,000 values take 10 minutes to render.


Code
ggplot(results, aes(x = players, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "red") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.002)) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Getting Four-of-a-Kind vs. Number of Players",
    x = "Number of Players",
    y = "Estimated Probability",
    caption = "Monte Carlo Simulation with n = 100,000 per player count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









In the above graph we see small variations in the probabilities for the different numbers of players. However, these variations are due to the (relatively) small sample size of 100,000 rounds, and re-running the simluation would give different numbers still distributed around 0.00168. With a larger sample size, we would expect to see less variation due to the law of large numbers.
Interestingly, the number of players in a poker game does not affect one’s odds of being dealt a four-of-a-kind. I had hypothesized otherwise, since more players playing means there is a higher chance that someone is dealt a card you need for a four-of-a-kind, but this conclusion demonstrates that it doesn’t make a difference if a card is in a different player’s hand or still in the deck after all the cards are dealt (since 45 cards will always not appear in your hand). If I was interested in getting a four-of-a-kind as quickly as possible, I could act on these findings by playing as many hands as possible with only one other player, since the probability of getting a four-of-a-kind in any given round is constant and each round would play quicker than compared to a game with 3 or more players.

title: Emissions
text:
This dataset comes from Carbon Majors, who have compiled a database of emissions data dating back to 1854. The dataset provides insights on the direct operational emissions of 122 of the world’s largest oil, gas, coal, and cement producers, with data such as entity type, commodity, production level, and total emissions attributed to that entity. I accessed it via the TidyTuesday repo from May 21, 2024.
The dataset can be found here: https://carbonmajors.org/Downloads
The TidyTuesday repo can be found here: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2024/2024-05-21
The following visualization shows the stark increase in the production of nearly every type of resource included in the dataset in recent years, except for thermal coal and natural gas. In addition, there is a clear major rise in oil, gas, coal, and cement production after around 1950, with production of most types increasing sharply until a little after 2000, at which point growth in production continues but at a lower rate.

title: Chess
text:
This dataset comes from Lichess.org via Mitchell J on Kaggle, representing over 20,000 games of chess collected from users on Lichess.org. Data includes players’ ratings, openings played, and outcome of the game (among other data). I accessed it via the TidyTuesday repo from October 1, 2024.
The dataset can be found here: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/datasnaek/chess/data
The TidyTuesday repo can be found here: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2024/2024-10-01
The following visualization shows the relationship between the number of turns a chess game takes and the difference between the two players’ ratings. A positive rating difference indicates that the player playing white had a higher rating than their opponent, and a negative rating difference indicates that the player playing black had a higher rating for that game. The visualization suggests that when there is a large difference between players’ ratings, fewer games with over 100 turns are played when compared to games where players’ have a small difference in ratings.

title: Ethics
text:
Ethics Discussion
In 2015, researchers published an dataset scraped from 60,000 OkCupid dating profiles. The following discussion explores the questions of ethics surrounding this incident.
The dataset was indeed for use in introductory data science classes, from which students could use to practice anonymization or discuss data science ethics (Xiao 2021). While the researchers may have had productive intentions, the publication of the dataset was of questionable ethicality. Although the researchers tried to anonymize the data, they collected many important identifiers that could be used to identify users. Additionally, the collection of data was against OkCupid’s policies, and users were unaware that their data could be used and published in such a way.
A similar incident occured in 2016 when Dutch researchers published a dataset scraped from 70,000 OkCupid profiles (Resnick 2016). The Dutch researchers made no attempt to anonymize the data, given all the information was already “public” since it was available online. However, others argue that publishing the information was unethical since the information is not entirely public in that it is intended only for other OkCupid users and the gathering of data was done without OkCupid’s permission. Another ethical questions arising from this situation is regarding academia. The Dutch researchers were able to publish this data through the Open Science Framework, a platform intended to increase transparency and decrease gatekeeping in academia. However, the potential for harm like in this case raises questions regarding whether we should decrease barriers in academia, or if they serve a valid, useful purpose.
Below I evaluate the processes used and identify the shortcomings of the OkCupid cases.
What is the permission / consent structure for using the data? Was it followed?
Consent is a freely given, informed, specific, and revocable agreement from a data subject that their information may be collected, analyzed, or shared for clearly stated purposes. Consent is important because it respects the autonomy and dignity of people and their information. No direct permission was received from OkCupid or from its users. The profiles were scraped from the website without any authorization. In addition, users could not have anticipated that their data would be published for use in an academic setting. This was a violation of the users’ autonomy and dignity in that it publicly exposed their personal information without their permission.
Is the data identifiable and sufficiently anonymized?
Identifiability is the ability to identify the source of data given the data points. Sufficiently anonymized data makes it so that people can not identify the exact entity from which the data came from. In cases where the data is regarding people, identifiability makes it so one can identify an individual based on their recorded characteristics, while anonymized data works to prevent this. In the OkCupid cases, the data was identifiable and not sufficiently anonymized, meaning that that one could identify certain individuals based on their reported characteristics, such as age, location, among other factors. The identifiability of the data violated users’ privacy since anyone interested could extract personal information about certain individuals from the dataset.
What was the data‑collection process, and was it ethical?
An ethical data-collection process should have protections for participants, ensure security of data, and result in anonymized data. The OkCupid data was collected via web‑scraping without platform approval, and arguably violated the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. It was not ethical since it was done without permission from any of the involved parties. The argument used by the Dutch researchers (that the information was already public) does not hold since the information was only partially public (only available for a target demographic to see). An ethical data-collection process would have required the permission of all users involved and the platform to ensure that only people who are okay with their information being published are included.
Were the data made publicly available, and are they being used in unintended ways?
Ideally, sensitive sensitive is shared only through a secure, access‑controlled repository under a license that restricts use to the specific, consented‑to purposes. The OkCupid data was made publicly available on the open web. Users’ personal essays, interests, and other identifying traits were freely downloadable. The release online meant that the data could be used for anything and everything beyond its intended classroom use. This constituted an ethical breach because it violates users’ peronal agency over their information (even if they consented to the study). The published information could be used for things like identifying people based on political beliefs or sexuality. A possible solution could be a gated-access model, in which access to the data could be regulated and controlled (Xiao 2021).
Citations

OK Cupid data release (privacy and publicly available data). Xiao, T., and Ma, Y. (2021), A Letter to the Journal of Statistics and Data Science Education — A Call for Review of ‘OkCupid Data for Introductory Statistics and Data Science Courses’ by Albert Y. Kim and Adriana Escobedo-Land, Journal of Statistics and Data Science Education, 29, 214–215.
Resnick, Brian. “Researchers Just Released Profile Data on 70,000 Okcupid Users without Permission.” Vox, Vox, 12 May 2016, www.vox.com/2016/5/12/11666116/70000-okcupid-users-data-release.

title: NYTimes Analysis
text:
Dataset: NYTimes Article Headlines
This analysis uses the NYTimes dataset from the RTextTools package. The dataset contains article IDs, publication dates, article headlines, article subjects, and topic codes for articles from the New York Times from 1996 to 2006. The dataset was compiled by Professor Amber E. Boydstun at the University of California, Davis.
The following graph shows the number of articles published each month from 1996-2006. Upon first inspection, February has the least number of articles published, and January, March, May, and December seem to have the most number of articles published. If we stop to consider why this might be, we quickly notice that February has the fewest days and January, March, May, and December all have 31 days. We inspect this further in the following graph.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(RTextTools)
data(NYTimes)
head(as_tibble(NYTimes), 4)


# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Article_ID Date     Title                                   Subject Topic.Code
       <int> <fct>    <fct>                                   <fct>        <int>
1      41246 1-Jan-96 Nation's Smaller Jails Struggle To Cop… Jails …         12
2      41257 2-Jan-96 FEDERAL IMPASSE SADDLING STATES WITH I… Federa…         20
3      41268 3-Jan-96 Long, Costly Prelude Does Little To Al… Conten…         20
4      41279 4-Jan-96 Top Leader of the Bosnian Serbs Now Un… Bosnia…         19


Code
#Adding a column onlyMonth that has extracts the "Jan" or similar from the date column using regular expressions. Converting this column into factors allows us to order the months chronologically. I grouped by this column and then plotted the number of articles published each month to get the following graph:
grouped_month <- NYTimes |> mutate(onlyMonth = factor(str_extract(Date, "(?<=-)[a-z|A-Z]+"), levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"))) |> group_by(onlyMonth)
#NYTimes <- fct_relevel(onlyMonth, levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"))
ggplot(grouped_month, aes(x = onlyMonth)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "", subtitle = "Number of Articles Published", title = "Number of Articles Published Each Month from 1996-2006")









The graph below more clearly shows that more articles are published during months with more days. Although we can’t prove why this is, the New York Times is published every day, meaning that months with more days likely have a higher quantity of articles simply because they have more editions published.


Code
#Groups the months based on the number of days in each month, and then computes the average number of articles published in each month in the period from 1996-2006.
new_grouped_month <- grouped_month |> mutate(numDays = ifelse(str_detect(onlyMonth, "Feb"), "28/29", ifelse(str_detect(onlyMonth, "Jan|Mar|May|Jul|Aug|Oct|Dec"), "31", "30"))) |> group_by(numDays) |> summarize(count = n()) |> mutate(average = ifelse(numDays == "31", count/7, ifelse(numDays == "30", count/4, count)))

ggplot(new_grouped_month, aes(x = numDays, y = average)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x="Number of Days in Month", y = "", subtitle = "Average Number of Articles Published", title = "Number of Articles Published Monthly Based on the Length of the Month")









The table below shows the most frequent lowercase words found in article headlines. Most of the words are very short in length, indicating that the New York Times prefers to keep words above 2-3 characters long capitalized. Notably, however, the words “special” and “report” both appear lowercased 34 times. Upon further inspection, I found that the New York Times ran an article series called “A special report”, reporting on important world-scale events. This series accounts for the otherwise strange appearance of these long lowercased words.


Code
lowercase <- NYTimes |> mutate(lowercase_words = str_extract_all(Title, "([^'-.\\&]\\b)[a-z][a-z|']*\\b")) |> unnest(lowercase_words) |> select(lowercase_words) |> mutate(lowercase_words = str_replace(lowercase_words, " ", "")) |> group_by(lowercase_words) |> summarize(count = n()) |> arrange(desc(count)) |> head(n=20) |> print()


# A tibble: 20 × 2
   lowercase_words count
   <chr>           <int>
 1 in                391
 2 to                346
 3 of                345
 4 the               319
 5 a                 287
 6 and               208
 7 for               195
 8 on                165
 9 at                 93
10 by                 55
11 as                 49
12 report             34
13 special            34
14 an                 32
15 but                23
16 or                 19
17 bin                 4
18 if                  4
19 is                  2
20 vs                  2


The graph below shows the number of election-related articles published in each month in the period 1996-2006. The graph shows spikes in election-related articles in the months January, May, July, September, October, and November. This spike in articles from September through November matches my expectations for the data, since elections in the US occur in November, and September and October are heavy campaigning months. I was surprised to see the spikes in January and May, which I hypothesize are attributable to inaugurations and primaries, respectively. Although there are relatively few election related articles represented here, it is clear that their publication usually occurs around the time of significant political/electoral events.


Code
election_articles <- grouped_month |> mutate(election = str_detect(Title, "elect|vote|voting") | str_detect(Subject, "elect|vote|voting")) |> group_by(onlyMonth) |> filter(election == TRUE)# |> summarize(count = n())
ggplot(election_articles, aes(x=onlyMonth)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x="Month", y = "", title = "Number of Election-Related Articles by Month from 1996-2006", subtitle = "Number of Articles")
